footer: Data: NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441) and NASA LRO LOLA topography. Times in UTC. Educational decision-support tool; it does not certify landing sites.

model_labels.reference_note: Meets the requirements in this model (0° horizon, no terrain). Real terrain can increase or reduce the hours.
model_labels.terrain_note: Uses the real horizon from LOLA topography, seen 2 m above the ground. Results apply to this exact point; a few meters away they can differ.
model_labels.no_terrain_warning: Terrain data is not available for this site. This does not mean the horizon is clear.

help.sun_elevation: How high the center of the Sun is above the horizon, in degrees. At the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so small hills matter.
help.azimuth: Compass direction: North 0°, East 90°, South 180°, West 270°.
help.sun_hours: Hours in the mission when the center of the Sun is above the horizon. This is illumination availability, not generated power: there is no solar panel model.
help.longest_gap_sun: Longest continuous stretch of the mission without the Sun. 'At least' means the stretch touches the start or end of the mission and may be longer.
help.earth_hours: Hours in the mission when the center of Earth is above the horizon. This is geometric visibility only: it does not guarantee a radio link.
help.longest_gap_earth: Longest continuous stretch of the mission without Earth in the sky.
help.both_hours: Hours when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon at the same time.
help.next_change: Time from the cursor until the next sunset/sunrise or Earthset/Earthrise. Hourly data: shown as ~N h, never with minutes.
help.requirements: Example requirements chosen by the team. Any requirement not met makes the scenario fail; a strong indicator never compensates for a failed one.
help.delay: Moves the landing date 7 days later and keeps the same duration, to see what changes.
help.region: Outlined boxes are the nine candidate regions NASA chose in October 2024 for the first crewed landing. Each region is about 16 to 77 km across and conditions change a lot inside it; the app shows one sample point per region, the most illuminated one in NASA's illumination map.
help.map: South pole maps: terrain from LOLA laser altimetry, shaded with an artificial light from the upper left to show its shape (not real sunlight). Global map: LRO Wide Angle Camera mosaic; dark areas are basalt plains (maria).

sources.title: Sun and Earth positions
sources.text: NASA/JPL Horizons System, DE441 ephemeris, observer on the Moon (MOON_ME frame, 1737.4 km sphere). Apparent azimuth and elevation with no atmospheric refraction (APPARENT=AIRLESS), one sample per hour. Lunar libration is included in the Horizons geometry.

sources.title: Terrain (all south pole sites)
sources.text: LRO LOLA elevation models. Connecting Ridge: 5 m/pixel Site01 map (Barker et al. 2021, NASA/GSFC PGDA product 78) plus the PDS LDEM_875S_20M and LDEM_80S_80M polar maps. Other south pole sites: PDS LDEM_85S_20M (20 m/pixel) plus LDEM_80S_80M. The horizon is the highest terrain angle in each direction, including the Moon's curvature. Sites far from the pole use a flat 0° horizon.

sources.title: Candidate landing regions
sources.text: Outlines of the nine regions NASA selected in October 2024 for the first crewed south pole landing (then planned as Artemis III; NASA now plans it as Artemis IV, in 2028), from the USGS data release by M. T. McClernan (2024), doi:10.5066/P1MEQ6UK, based on LROC QuickMap. In each region the app uses one sample point: the most illuminated pixel in NASA's LOLA average illumination map. It is a team choice for comparison, not a landing site.

sources.title: Validation of the terrain horizon
sources.text: Compared with published illumination studies of the lunar south pole: Glaser et al. 2018 (Planetary and Space Science 162) for the Connecting Ridge, and the LOLA average illumination and Earth visibility maps of Mazarico et al. 2011 (Icarus 211) for every south pole site. Periods and resolutions differ, so the agreement shows consistency, not equality.

sources.title: Maps and site context
sources.text: Global map: LRO Wide Angle Camera global mosaic served by NASA Moon Trek (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University). South pole maps: shaded relief from the LOLA polar elevation maps. Site coordinates from LROC image releases, Glaser et al. 2018 and the NASA NSSDC Apollo site list (each site lists its own source).

sources.title: Space agency partner context
sources.text: Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Moon Exploration portal, for the educational context on lunar missions. The Chandrayaan-3 site comes from the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) mission.

sources.title: Use of AI tools
sources.text: Parts of the data-processing code were written with AI coding assistants (Claude by Anthropic; Codex by OpenAI) following the team's specification, and reviewed by the team. Results come from fixed rules, not from generative AI.

simplifications: Visible means the center of the body is above the horizon.
Hourly samples with linear interpolation: event times are rounded to the hour.
Without terrain data, the horizon is a flat 0° line from a smooth sphere.
No solar panel, battery, antenna or radio link model.
Requirements are team demonstration assumptions, not NASA criteria.
Periods outside the data coverage show 'Insufficient data'; values are never extrapolated.
general_facts: A full day on the Moon (sunrise to sunrise) lasts about 709 hours, or 29.5 Earth days.
The Moon has no atmosphere: no refraction lifts the Sun near the horizon, so the horizon is set only by terrain and the Moon's curvature.
The Moon's axis is tilted only about 1.5°, so near the poles the Sun skims the horizon all year and small terrain changes decide between light and darkness.

facts: Here the Sun never climbs more than 2.1° above a flat horizon. Any terrain rising more than 2.1° in its direction would hide it all year.
Earth rises and sets here because of libration: it is above the horizon 53% of the year, and the longest wait without it is 13.4 days.
With a flat 0° horizon the Sun would be hidden for 164.6 days in a row. The real terrain seen from 2 m above the ground cuts that to 11.9 days: the Sun is visible 86% of the year instead of 52%.
